detail.body: ## Overview In Tiered Offloading, the CPU block allocation for Secondary -> Primary transfer happens in tiering/manager.py. Under load, this leads to, reserving / locking the CPU cache space for long periods of time unnecessarily. For example, when the FS tier has only N threads, we'd only need to allocate space for N jobs for active use. This behavior on `main` makes "Promotion Allocation Failure" a function of input requests load. ## Claims This PR adds a Lazy CPU block allocation technique, by which the FS tier allocates CPU blocks only when it needs it. With this "Promotion Allocation Failure" becomes a function of the number of FS read/write threads. Users can tune their FS read/write threads value based on their CPU KV cache size. Note : With Thread Pool batching https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/58404 "Promotion Allocation Failure" will further be decoupled from RW thread count. With batching, there is only a small constant number of jobs that are actively promoting at any given time. ## Validation [bench.sh](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33185797/bench.sh) Benchmarking Setup: Model : gptoss120b GPU : H100 x 2 CPU KV Cache size : 25GB GPU mem util : 0.7 Benchmark : Guidellm - Multiturn conversations - 5 Turns, 20K prefix, 4K subsequent ISL . Concurrency 64 PR vs main (best) |   |   |   |   -- | -- | -- | -- | --   |   | TTFT   | Total tokens / s | Mean | P50 | P95 PR Best (num_rw_threads = 4) | 181K | 11.2s | 11.4s | 17.5s Main Best (num_rw_threads = 4) | 138K | 14.6s | 13.8s | 23.3s RW threads sweeps |   |   -- | -- | --   | Main | PR rw threads | Total Tokens / s | Total Tokens / s 16 | 120,944.50 | 120,891.10 8 | 122,463.90 | 115,491.50 4 | 138,062.50 | 181,032.50 Note that that the CPU kv cache space acquired by the FS tiers scales down with the number of read/write threads used in the FS tier. ## Details Changes: - LazyTransferJob : subclass TransferJob to introduce LazyTransferJob. A dataclass that inputs a "allocation function" and materializes the CPU cache blocks only when requested. - Lock Primary Tier accesses: In the PR, the FS tier threads are responsible for making the actual allocation calls. This interferes with the Scheduler thread launched GPU <-> CPU transfer allocations. As a result, the primary tier accesses from the TieringManager is always guarded by a lock. - TieringManager::_scheduler_hit_threads : The allocation by the FS threads should not evict an on-going lookup for a request. _scheduler_hit_threads records the current request lookups and protects them from a FS evict due to allocation. - Metrics : Due to the fact that the allocation is lazy, `PROMOTION_ALLOCATION_FAILURE` and `primary_write_chunk_count` are updated during the allocation for the LazyTransferJobs. For Eager jobs (i.e. eagerly allocated) the behavior remains the same as on `main`. - Note that the changes only affect the FS tier. Although, the framework for other Secondary tiers to follow suite is established with this PR. ## Testing: Added unit tests - passes locally. ### lm-eval tests [eval.sh](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33187218/eval.sh) `./eval.sh 4-gpu-cpu-nvme gptoss120b ` model : gptoss-120b Methodology: perform lm-eval 3 times with GPU and CPU cache reset after each lm-eval. #### PR: ``` Run1 : Stores KV to FS tier |Tasks|Version| Filter |n-shot| Metric | |Value | |Stderr| |-----|------:|----------------|-----:|-----------|---|-----:|---|-----:| |gsm8k| +            keys=all_keys,
+            chunk_ids=None,

+        assert list(job.chunk_ids) == [0, 1, 2, 3]
+
+        # Half cached

+        job = PromotionTransferJob(
+            job_id=11,
+            req_context=_CTX,
+            keys=all_keys,
+            chunk_ids=None,
+            alloc_fn=lambda req_keys, ctx: (
+                list(uncached),
+                np.array([0, 1], dtype=np.int32),
+            ),
+        )
+        tier.submit_load(job)
+        result = drain(tier)[0]
+        assert result.success is True
+        assert set(job.keys) == set(uncached)
+        assert list(job.chunk_ids) == [0, 1]
+
+        # All cached

+            job_id=12,
+            req_context=_CTX,
+            keys=all_keys,

+        assert len(list(job.chunk_ids)) == 0
+
+    def test_promotion_fs_file_availability(self, fs_tier):
+        """FS file availability determines promotion success and partial-success
+        reporting.
+
+        Three sub-cases, each using its own keys and non-overlapping chunk slots:
+          - All files present:  full success, successful_keys is None.
+          - Half files present: partial failure, successful_keys holds the loaded half.
+          - No files present:   immediate failure, successful_keys is None.

+        # All files present → full success

+
+        # Half files deleted; partial failure
+        # Delete files for key(3) and key(4); key(1) and key(2) remain on disk.

+        job = PromotionTransferJob(

+                np.array([0, 1, 2, 3], dtype=np.int32),
+            ),
+        )
+        tier.submit_load(job)
+        result = drain(tier)[0]
+        assert result.success is False
+        assert result.successful_keys is not None
+        assert set(result.successful_keys) == {key(1), key(2)}
+        # job.keys reflects the full originally-requested set, not just what loaded
+        assert set(job.keys) == set(all_keys)
+        assert list(job.chunk_ids) == [0, 1, 2, 3]
+
+        # All files deleted → nothing loaded
+        for k in all_keys[:2]:
+            path = tier.file_mapper.get_file_name(k)
+            if os.path.exists(path):
+                os.remove(path)
+
+        job = PromotionTransferJob(
+            job_id=22,
+            req_context=_CTX,
+            keys=all_keys,
+            chunk_ids=None,
+            alloc_fn=lambda req_keys, ctx: (
+                list(req_keys),
+                np.array([0, 1, 2, 3], dtype=np.int32),
+            ),
+        )
+        tier.submit_load(job)
+        result = drain(tier)[0]
+        assert result.success is False
+        assert result.successful_keys is None  # nothing loaded before the first failure
+        # job.keys still reflects the full originally-requested set
+        assert set(job.keys) == set(all_keys)
+        assert list(job.chunk_ids) == [0, 1, 2, 3]

Hi @orozery 

I assume the suggestion is to, 
 - Defer CPU block allocation to _flush_pending_promotions, and
 - Submit only as many load jobs as dictated by the tier's max_inflight_promotion_jobs

I think it'd be better to not add another optimization parameter vertical with `max_inflight_promotion_jobs`. 

A `max_inflight_promotion_jobs` requires tuning the parameter for 
 1. CPU KV cache size : We want to use CPU tier judiciously so we dont drop promotions / cascades unnecessarily. A max_inflight_promotion_jobs for a small CPU KV cache is not optimal for a bigger CPU KV cache. For a bigger CPU KV cache, we could allow a more inflight promotions.
 2. Secondary Tier medium (nvme, remote-disks, object-tier etc.) : We want to Exercise the Secondary tier for maximum bandwidth. The max_inflight_promotion_jobs parameter should be such that the submitted jobs keep the Tier active between forward passes.  
 3. Model (model forward pass time) - This dictates the frequency with which we call the flush.
 4. Workload (big vs small requests)

For this instance, I believe we may avoid tuning by letting the runtime workload drive the pressure. 

The crux of the issue really is the over-reservation of CPU blocks. Allocating the blocks only when necessary, lets the Engine (Model) / Workload drive the CPU KV cache space required and the Tiers are not artificially throttled. 

Further, there is a FS threadpool batching argument to this (Planned as a followup). On the PR, each FS thread picks up a job. This is sub-optimal. With batching,  where each promotion job is split across multiple threads, we'd only need to allocate CPU KV cache space for a few jobs at a time. This will drive down the CPU space requirements further, tying a Job's CPU KV cache pinning duration to model forward pass time.

I think there are benefits in letting the tiers handle CPU allocation as they see fit and in letting the system drive the requirements naturally. Pre-allocating, is simpler, but I think with that, we will always need to fight the Promotion / Cascade Allocation Failure performance issues. 

I realize the complexity the PR introduces. I am happy to discuss / re-work implementation. Thanks 🙌
